question.text: An investor holds units in a Regular Plan and wants to switch to the Direct Plan of the same scheme. What are the implications?

answer.text: The switch is treated as a mere administrative change with no tax or NAV impact
The switch is treated as a redemption from the Regular Plan and a fresh purchase in the Direct Plan, and taxes/loads may apply like a normal redemption-cum-purchase
The switch is not allowed by SEBI — investors must redeem and then separately invest in the Direct Plan
The switch automatically converts existing units without any redemption transaction

explanation.text: The Logic: Per NISM Series V-A (p.166), an investor may switch out from one scheme/plan to another, including from the Regular Plan to the Direct Plan of the same scheme. Per p.181 and p.204, a switch is defined as a redemption from one option/plan/scheme combined with a fresh purchase in another. Per p.156, p.160, and p.203, capital gains tax (and STT, in the case of equity-oriented schemes) can apply to a redemption/switch transaction depending on the scheme type and holding period. The Trap: Options A and D treat the switch as a non-transaction. The source treats a switch as a redemption + purchase, so it can have the same tax and load implications as any other redemption-cum-purchase. Option C is wrong — the switch is allowed; it is simply not tax-neutral. Note: Exit-load applicability depends on the scheme's load structure and the holding period at the time of switch.
